candidate_decisions.reason: All eleven nominated focus branches land in the integrated names-and-voice finding. The host basmala and 17:111 provide native context for the one-referent reading; the vocal bounds and sought path remain explicit components.

The 17:97 guidance, speechlessness, and lost-hearing coordinates match the supplied lean context occurrences and return through the focus voice limits and sought path. The result is retained as qualified attributed context, with the eschatological alternative explicit.

The 17:100 treasury, mercy, withholding, expenditure, and constriction coordinates match the lean context; the focus al-Rahman and invocation supply the return. The full before/after change and the alternative reading of 17:100 are preserved.

All five traced branches land through 17:101-102 and the focus names. The physical-mark branch is retained as an identifying-function analogy with its literal restriction stated; unresolved context branches remain attributed, and the Moses-only alternative and no-value connection reviews remain visible.

The complete 17:106-107 and 17:109 trace returns through the focus prayer, paired vocal limits, and sought path. Its added cadence, audience-reception, and embodied-response reading survives with the narrower loudness-only alternative and legacy attribution explicit.

Its one-referent reading is the exact naming component carried by macro:names-and-voice. Every supplied branch role, including the unresolved 17:111 denials and magnification trace, is retained there with attributed mode; no branch, context, or obligation is excluded.

findings.title: Many names, one referent, a sought voice path
findings.claim: Allah and al-Rahman are distinct addresses whose beautiful names belong to one addressee: the focus assigns the plural names to the singular Him, the host basmala places Allah and al-Rahman together, and 17:111 denies offspring, partner, and dependent protector before magnification. In the same focus, loudness and muting bound a vocal way that must be actively sought.
findings.mechanism: The repeated invocation keeps the act constant while its named object varies; the open choice of name and the fronted singular lahu meet in the plural al-asma al-husna. The host basmala supplies the same names in one formula, and the immediate 17:111 closure denies lineage, co-ownership, and divided sovereignty before commanding magnification. Separately, la tajhar and la tukhafit set two vocal limits, while ibtaghi bayna dhalika sabilan turns those limits into a positive search for a way between them.
findings.reader_payoff: Plural divine names need not multiply their bearer, and the voice instruction is an active practice of finding a way between two prohibited edges rather than a single fixed command about loudness.
findings.containment: The one-referent reading is anchored in the focus pronoun and the adjacent 17:111 denials; a live alternative is that 17:111 is an independent doxology. The HFT trace's finer roles for child, partner, sovereignty, and magnification remain attributed because those branch records are unresolved. The finding does not prescribe a decibel level or make the varied names competing owners.

epistemic.reason: The trusted channel supports and the focus grammar directly grounds the naming and vocal relations. The represented HFT trace has complete supplied anchors but legacy_unbound reader identity and unresolved context branches, so its additional roles are retained as attributed evidence.

findings.title: A guided path that preserves audibility
findings.claim: The pericope's pairing of guidance with lost speech and hearing gives the focus's sought path between raised and hushed prayer an additional communicative edge: it can preserve a relation in which speech remains receivable.
findings.mechanism: In 17:97, guidance toward a way stands beside the gathered people's inability to speak or hear. In 17:110, the prayer is bounded by two vocal prohibitions and a positively sought path. Their contact changes a reading concerned only with the worshipper's volume into one that also attends to whether speech can reach and be received.
findings.reader_payoff: The middle path becomes a relation between speaking and hearing, not merely a location on the speaker's volume scale.
findings.containment: The 17:97 disabilities belong to an eschatological scene and may not specify prayer technique; this is the HFT's attributed contextual inference. It does not claim the focus prayer is silent, that 17:97 gives a ritual prescription, or that one vocal level is correct.

epistemic.reason: Every trace coordinate agrees with the supplied 17:97 lean root occurrences and returns through focus words for raised voice, lowered voice, and path. The HFT reader identity is legacy_unbound and its own live alternative is retained.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: The sought vocal way can preserve speech that remains available for reception.
branch_activations.boundary: The branch registry is unresolved; the HFT role is retained without a gloss or facet.

findings.title: Mercy approached, not possessed
findings.claim: The reading of al-Rahman expands from a permissible alternate name to an address through mercy as non-hoarded abundance: 17:100 places treasuries of mercy beside a human impulse to hold back, while 17:110 makes invocation an approach to the named source and assigns the names to Him.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier al-Rahman and its repeated calling meet 17:100's treasury of mercy, fear of expenditure, withholding, and constriction. The contrast changes the name from one allowed label in a naming choice into an address to mercy that is approached rather than possessed or depleted by use.
findings.reader_payoff: The name al-Rahman carries the feel of generosity that can be called upon without being treated as a finite stock the caller owns.
findings.containment: The treasury passage describes a hypothetical human response and may only characterize human stinginess, without explaining the later invocation. The non-hoarding contact is an attributed pericope inference; it does not claim that mercy is a material resource or that 17:100 dictates how to pray.

epistemic.reason: The complete HFT trace's context ayah, indices, and roots agree with the supplied 17:100 lean occurrences and return through the focus al-Rahman and invocation. Its reader identity remains legacy_unbound, and the source's human-character alternative is preserved.

branch_activations.activation: The attributed treasury image meets the mercy-name and its owner, producing an image of mercy held in reserve rather than possessed by the caller.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus invocation approaches mercy that is not depleted by being named.
branch_activations.boundary: The branch registry is unresolved; no gloss or facet is supplied.

findings.title: Beautiful names as signs of recognition
findings.claim: The focus's beautiful names can be read as identifying signs through which their addressee becomes recognizable: 17:101 calls Moses' signs clear, 17:102 calls them insights, and the focus names are the carrier that receives this recognitional pressure.
findings.mechanism: The focus name-set and its goodness adjective meet the pericope's explicit signs, clarification, and inward insight. The HFT's mark branch contributes its identifying function by analogy, so a list of beautiful names becomes legible as a set of indicators through which one referent is recognized.
findings.reader_payoff: The names can be heard as doing more than naming: they make the addressee recognizable to a receptive hearer.
findings.containment: The live alternative is that the signs and insight describe Moses alone and do not alter divine naming; the supplied connection reviews for 17:101 and 17:102 report no distinct link. The physical-mark branch is used only for its identifying function by analogy, not as a claim that divine names are literal brands. The unresolved context branches remain attributed.

epistemic.reason: The HFT anchor set is complete and the context roots and word indices match the supplied lean records. However, the HFT reader identity is legacy_unbound, the context morphology is not supplied, and the sign-to-name contact is an inference kept alongside the Moses-only counter-reading.

branch_activations.activation: The attributed manifest-sign role meets the names as identifying designations and returns through the focus name-set.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus names can function as readable indicators of their referent.

findings.title: Prayer with pace, audibility, and uptake
findings.claim: The sought way for prayer's voice can include cadence and reception as well as a place between loudness extremes: the focus's paired limits meet 17:106's divided, unhurried recitation to people and 17:107-109's prostration, tears, and growing humility.
findings.mechanism: The focus actively seeks a way between raised and hushed prayer sound. The preceding passage describes recitation divided for delivery to people at leisure, then recitation followed by prostration, weeping, and increased humility. These separate carriers and responses make the focus's middle way a paced, differentiated delivery that can reach hearers and ripen into embodied receptivity.
findings.reader_payoff: The instruction is perceptible as a vocal practice shaped by timing and listener uptake, with humility as a possible response, rather than as a single volume setting.

findings.title: Invocation meets exclusive worship
findings.claim: In the added recitation lens, the focus call to Allah meets Fatiha 1:5's explicit worship and appeal for help directed to one addressee, adding a concrete devotional act to the names chosen for invocation.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier is Allah as the object of ud'u. External 1:2 names Allah as the one praised, and the following 1:5 addresses that referent as You alone in worship and the request for aid; the named invocation thus contacts an explicit act of exclusive worship and dependence.
findings.reader_payoff: The choice of divine address is heard as leading into a direct act of worship and help-seeking, not as a naming exercise by itself.
findings.containment: This overlay uses the ordered external members 1:2 and 1:5 only. The second-person pronoun in 1:5 is linked to Allah through 1:2; it is not a lexical definition of Allah, does not specify the focus's voice level, and does not import a whole-surah path system.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch nomination is marked trusted and both external ayat are supplied verbatim with root occurrences. The cross-ayah link from the named referent in 1:2 to the exclusive act in 1:5 is an ordered-context inference without a separate connection record.
